title: When Qualitron Failed, Stan Shih Started Multitech on NT$1 Million
dek: In 1976, forced out of a failing calculator maker, Stan Shih and colleagues started a small microprocessor firm and chose from the start to share it.

story.event: Founding Multitech around microprocessors after leaving the failing Qualitron
story.summary: In the second half of 1976, as the Taiwanese calculator maker Qualitron sank into financial trouble, its vice-president Stan Shih and two research colleagues left and founded Multitech with NT$1 million (about US$25,000), aiming at the new microprocessor market. Shih and his wife Carolyn Yeh held half the company and partners the rest, a deliberate break from family ownership; the firm traded chips, consulted, ran a microprocessor training centre and later became Acer.
paragraphs: In the second half of 1976, Stan Shih was vice-president of Qualitron, a Taiwanese calculator maker he had helped set up four years earlier, responsible for its research, manufacturing, business development and purchasing. Before that, at Unitron, he had designed Taiwan's first desktop calculator, a milestone that did not sell well. By his own account in his memoir, Me-Too Is Not My Style, Qualitron's financial problems had by now become "irremediable", and he and two research colleagues, George Huang and Fred Lin, had to leave.

Shih wrote that they "hastily founded Multitech with the initial target being the new microprocessor market." Acer's records put the starting capital at NT$1 million, about US$25,000, and the work at trading, product design and advising others on using microprocessor technology. The company began with eleven employees and in its early days distributed chips to Taiwanese makers of arcade games. Shih later said its first two years were the only ones in its first decade that were not profitable.

How the company would be owned was decided early as well. Shih and his wife, Carolyn Yeh, who kept its first books, held half; partners held the rest, and he later made clear that his three children would not be given jobs there. "Our original plan, when we started, was to be decentralized," he told an interviewer in 1996, calling it contrary to the Chinese tradition of family-owned firms. When Multitech opened branches in Taichung and Kaohsiung in 1979, a local partner owned 60 per cent of them; "we saw that it worked, it made money," he said.

The company also taught. In 1978, by Acer's own count, it set up a Microprocessor Training Centre that trained 3,000 engineers for Taiwan's information industry. Its first branded product, in 1981, was the MicroProfessor-I, a small computer for learning to program a Z80 processor, made to sit on a shelf like a book. Multitech was later renamed Acer. Asked in 1996 how he measured success, Shih said "the number of people you are able to train is a contribution."

quote.text: And the extent of their association is the extent of their friendship, as it is the extent to which justice exists between them.
quote.source_title: Nicomachean Ethics, tr. W. D. Ross, The Internet Classics Archive (MIT)
quote.connection: Aristotle measures a bond by how much the people in it actually share. Shih's hurried start left him little money, but his first choices widened what Multitech shared: half the company to partners outside his family, majority stakes to local partners, and training for engineers across Taiwan's industry.

reflection: Multitech did not begin at a moment Shih chose. The company he had helped build was failing, and he wrote that the new one was founded in haste. Yet the decisions that lasted were not hasty ones: who would own it, how far control would be shared, and who would be taught.

Much of your own work may start under pressure, on someone else's timetable, and that part is rarely yours to set. What stays yours, even on a rushed day, is how widely you share what you know and whom you build with. Shih counted the people he trained as part of his contribution. The colleague you patiently showed a method last month belongs on that list too.
invitation: Think of one thing you know how to do that a colleague keeps asking you about. Today, spend ten unhurried minutes showing them how, and let that count as real work.

cross_checks.claim: Multitech was founded in 1976 with about US$25,000 (NT$1 million) in capital
Shih had helped set up Qualitron and was its vice-president before leaving to found Multitech in 1976
Multitech's early business was microprocessor-centred: trading and distributing chips and advising on microprocessor technology
Ownership was deliberately spread beyond the Shih family, against the tradition of family-owned firms
The MicroProfessor-I of 1981, a computer for learning Z80 programming, was the company's first branded product

research_notes: Founding date: Acer's own timeline gives 1 August 1976; the Computer History Museum record and the IT History Society give September 1976; Shih's memoir says the second half of 1976. The story says 'the second half of 1976'. Number of founders disagrees: CHM and IT History say four partners including Carolyn Yeh; EBSCO says Yeh and three others; The Irish Times (1997) says Shih and Yeh owned half and five partners the rest; the HomeComputerMuseum says Yeh and five partners. The story names only the two colleagues Shih names in his memoir (George Huang, Fred Lin) and says 'partners held the rest' without a count. Capital is consistent (NT$1 million, about US$25,000). Early business: Acer says trade, product design and microprocessor consultancy; strategy+business calls it a chip distributor for arcade-game makers; Reference for Business says it began by designing hand-held electronic games and then distributed imported semiconductors. The story uses Acer's description and the strategy+business detail. Headquarters: IT History and the HomeComputerMuseum say Hsinchu, while Shih in 1996 spoke of 'the Taipei part of the company' in 1979, so the story names no founding city (the slate's 'in Taipei' is not asserted). Renaming: Acer says the name was created in 1987; IT History says 1989; Reference for Business says 1981; the story says only 'later renamed Acer'. The Microprocessor Training Centre and its 3,000 engineers come only from Acer's own timeline, so the story attributes the figure to Acer. The children's exclusion is reported by The Irish Times (1997) and Reference for Business without a date, so the story says he 'later made clear' it. The memoir itself is not online; its wording is taken from the excerpt quoted on the Calcuseum Qualitron page. Shih's 'first two years' remark is from the 1996 interview, where he said the company doubled revenue every year in its first ten years and only the first two were unprofitable. The Aristotle passage comes from Book VIII, chapter 9, on friendship and justice in every kind of community or association, applied here by analogy to a business partnership. The founder field was shortened from "Stan Shih and Carolyn Yeh, with partners" to "Stan Shih and Carolyn Yeh" because the repeat screen flagged (but passed) an unrelated edition whose founder field also contains "founding partners"; it is a different person and company.
